abstract: Summary Cysteine post-translational modifications are important for protein functions and protein-protein interactions. Here, we present a protocol to detect the reversibly oxidized and reduced cysteine residues of proteins using differential alkylation labeling techniques with liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis. We describe steps for tissue sample preparation, differential alkylation, trypsin digestion, and LC-MS analysis. We then detail procedures for protein identification and data analysis. This protocol has potential application in pinpointing the modified cysteine residues in organs and cells in various disease models. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Oo et al. 1

Step-by-step method details
Labeling of reduced and oxidized cysteine residues by differential alkylation
Timing: 1 day
1.
Protein extraction from the tissue samples.
a.
Add 500 μL of pre-chilled
Tissue lysis buffer
to the 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube.
b.
Put the frozen tissue pieces into the tube.
c.
Homogenize with a handheld tissue grinder on ice until there are no visible tissue pieces.
d.
Transfer the homogenates to the new 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes.
e.
Sonicate 10 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C.
f.
Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 30 minutes at 4°C, collect the supernatant.
g.
Measure the protein concentration of each sample using DC Protein Assay Kit II from BIO-RAD.
i.
Prepare Reagent A′ by mixing Reagent A and Reagent S in 50:1 ratio.
ii.
Prepare and dilute Albumin protein standard (2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625 μg/ μL).
iii.
Prepare sample dilutions (2 to 3 times dilution).
iv.
Dispense 25 μL of Reagent A′, 5 μL of standards/samples, and 200 μL of Reagent B sequentially into each well of transparent 96-well plate.
v.
Incubate 15 minutes at room temperature and measure the absorbance at 650–750 nm.
2.
Labeling cysteine thiols (reduced cysteine residues) using N-ethylmaleimide (NEM).
a.
Prepare the 50 mL conical centrifuge tube for each sample and cover it with aluminum foil.
b.
Prepare and dilute the samples with
PBS buffer, pH 7.3,
to obtain a total protein of 2 mg per sample, and add NEM as the same mass as the protein content, with the final volume of 1 mL.
c.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
3.
Protein precipitation using methanol/chloroform.
a.
Add 4 mL of methanol to 1 mL volume of the previous sample mix and vortex for 10 seconds.
b.
Add 1 mL of chloroform to the sample and vortex for 10 seconds.
c.
Add 3 mL of ultrapure water (the sample should look cloudy) and vortex for 10 seconds.
d.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 2 minutes at room temperature.
e.
Discard the top aqueous layer. Protein exists between layers and is visible as a thin wafer.
f.
Add 4 mL of methanol and vortex for 10 seconds.
g.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 3 minutes at room temperature.
h.
Remove as much methanol as possible without disturbing the pellet.
i.
Open the lid of the tube and incubate at 37°C for 3 minutes to dry.
4.
Labeling of the oxidized cysteine residues using biotin-PEAC5-maleimide (BPM).
a.
Resuspend the pellet in 426.8 μL of 5 mM
TCEP solution, pH 7.7
.
b.
Incubate at 56°C for 30 minutes, followed by 15 minutes at room temperature.
c.
Add 73.2 μL of
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide stock solution
(Final biotin-PEAC5-maleimide concentration: 2.5 mM in 500 μL).
d.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
e.
Add 426.8 μL of 5 mM
TCEP solution, pH 7.7.
f.
Add 73.2 μL of
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide stock solution.
g.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
5.
Protein precipitation using methanol/chloroform.
a.
Add 4 mL of methanol to 1 mL of the previous sample mix and vortex for 10 seconds.
b.
Add 1 mL of chloroform to the sample and vortex for 10 seconds.
c.
Add 3 mL of ultrapure water (the sample should look cloudy) and vortex for 10 seconds
d.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 2 minutes at room temperature.
e.
Discard the top aqueous layer. Protein exists between layers and is visible as a thin wafer.
f.
Add 4 mL of methanol and vortex for 10 seconds.
g.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 3 minutes at room temperature.
h.
Remove as much methanol as possible without disturbing the pellet
i.
Open the lid of the tube and incubate at 37°C for 3 minutes to dry.
CRITICAL:
All these steps require protection from light to prevent degradation of the biotin-peac5-maleimide, n-ethylmaleimide, and to avoid unwanted side reactions.
Note:
N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) completes its reaction kinetics within 15 minutes at neutral pH, and the reaction is irreversible.
5
,
6
Furthermore, its rapid reaction rate reduces the need to use large molar excesses.
6
This offers a significant advantage over one of the most common alkylating reagents, the haloalkane iodoacetamide (IAM), which requires a basic pH (above pH 8)
7
and incubation times of 4 to 6 h with a large molar excess of IAM (up to 1000 times that of protein cysteine).
8
Additionally, the reactions with IAM to form thioethers are often incomplete under these conditions and are not irreversible.
9
,
10
Note:
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide (BPM) has a shorter and less bulky spacer arm, which reduces steric hindrance and makes it a more compact label in comparison to Maleimide-PEG2/11-maleimide. This compactness enhances accessibility to buried cysteine residues.
Pause point:
At this point, the peptide samples can be stored at 4°C for less than 24 h or at −80°C for less than one month.
In-solution trypsin digestion of labeled proteins
Timing: 3 days
6.
Denaturation of proteins by urea.
a.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 μL of
Trypsin digestion buffer with urea.
b.
Sonicate 5 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C.
c.
Incubate at 60°C for 1 hour.
d.
Allow the samples to cool down at room temperature (about 15 min).
e.
Add 3.5 mL of
Trypsin digestion buffer
(to decrease the urea concentration to 1 M).
f.
Sonicate 5 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C (Repeat this step until there are no insoluble substances that can be seen by the naked eye).
g.
Determine the protein concentration as in Step 1G.
h.
Transfer 1 mg of denatured proteins to new 50 mL conical centrifuge tubes.
7.
Digestion of denatured proteins by trypsin.
a.
Add 16.7 μg (41.75 μL) of sequencing-grade trypsin (1:60, 1 μg of Trypsin for 60 μg of protein) to each tube.
b.
Incubate at 37°C for 16 hours (can extend up to 18 hours).
c.
Add 16.7 μg (41.75 μL) of sequencing-grade trypsin to each tube again.
d.
Incubate at 37°C for 4 hours.
e.
Stop the trypsin digestion activity by adding
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
to the digestion mix until the solution reaches a pH below 4.
f.
Use a pH test strip to verify the pH of the solution. (2–3 times the volume of the sample mix may be needed).
8.
Concentration of digested peptides by vacuum centrifugation.
a.
Aliquot the sample mix to 1.5 mL centrifuge tubes (up to 1 mL in each 1.5 mL centrifuge tube).
b.
Centrifuge at 20,000 x g for 20 minutes at room temperature.
c.
Transfer the supernatant (about 500 μL) to a new 1.5 mL centrifuge tube.
d.
Resuspend the pellet in the previous 1.5 mL centrifuge tube by adding 100 μL of
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
and pipetting.
e.
Centrifuge at 20,000 x g for 20 minutes at room temperature.
f.
Transfer the supernatant (about 500 μL) to a new 1.5 mL centrifuge tube (Do not disturb the pellet).
g.
Concentrate each sample by vacuum centrifugation (SpeedVac) until only jelly-like fluid remains (may take up to 18–24 hours to dry).
CRITICAL:
It is crucial to open the microcentrifuge tube caps when speed-vacuuming to allow the solvent to evaporate.
CRITICAL:
The samples may suck out when the centrifugation is turned off prior to pressure stabilization. Let the pressure equalize before turning off the centrifugation to take out the samples.
Pause point:
At this point, the peptide samples can be stored at 4°C for less than 24 h or at −80°C for less than one month.
9.
Resuspension of dry peptides.
a.
Resuspend all fractions of the peptide samples with
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
to obtain 2.4 μg/μL (Resuspend all fractions [Total protein 1 mg] with 416.7 μL of
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
.
b.
Take 42 μL from the combined sample and continue for LC-MS analysis (total 100 μg of peptides).
Peptide handling and preparation for liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
Timing: 6–8 h
10.

a.
Remove and discard the protective white tip at the bottom of the column included in the Pierce High pH Reversed-Phase Peptide Fractionation Kit.
b.
Put the column into a 2 mL sample tube.
c.
Centrifuge the tube at 5000 x g for 2 minutes to pack the resin material.
d.
Discard the liquid.
e.
Load 300 μL of acetonitrile into the column.
f.
Centrifuge at 5000 x g for 2 minutes.
g.
Discard the flow-through acetonitrile and repeat steps ‘f’ and ‘g’.
h.
Wash the spin column twice with 300 μL of
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
.
i.
Centrifuge at 5000 x g for 2 minutes.
j.
Discard the 0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution and repeat step ‘g’.
Note:
Each sample needs 300 μL of elution solution. For fractionating more than three samples, prepare enough volumes of the elution solutions for all samples.

11.
Resuspend peptides for LC-MS analysis.
a.

LC-MS/MS reconstitution buffer

b.

c.

d.
Inject 5 μL (83.3 μg of peptide amount) of each sample into the mass spectrometer for analysis.

body:
Before you begin
We recently established a differential alkylation labeling method that enables pinpointing oxidized and reduced cysteine residues in brown adipose tissue
1
(
Figure 1
). Traditionally, several studies have utilized a biotin-maleimide to alkylate the oxidized cysteine residues and enrich them using avidin-family proteins for LC-MS analysis.
2
,
3
,
4
When combined with tandem mass tags, this approach allows for quantification of the proportion of oxidized cysteine residues. In contrast, our protocol offers a direct method for analyzing both oxidized and reduced cysteine residues without the need for avidin-based enrichment prior to LC-MS analysis. This strategy not only facilitates the detection of cysteine residues modified by oxidative stress but also those affected by reductive stress under specific conditions. Since modifications of cysteine residues can significantly influence protein structure, function, and protein-protein interactions, comprehensive identification of both oxidized and reduced forms is essential for understanding their roles in proteins, metabolic pathways, and physiological processes. The success of this technique relies on both the pH of the buffer solutions used during labeling and the protection of samples from light. Therefore, it is critical to carefully adjust the buffer pH and ensure adequate light protection before beginning the experiment. The following protocol outlines the steps for preparing samples for cysteine redoxome analysis in mouse brown adipose tissue. With optimized conditions, this method can also be extended to other tissues (such as liver, and muscle) and to adherent cells in various disease models.
Figure 1
Overview of steps involved in pinpointing oxidized and reduced cysteine residues in various samples
Innovation
This protocol introduces alternative strategies to simultaneously profile oxidized and reduced cysteine residues across diverse mouse tissues and cell lines under different pathological and stress conditions. By enabling comprehensive detection of both oxidized and reduced states, our methodology expands the characterization of cysteine redox modifications and complements existing approaches to define the cysteine proteome in both physiological and disease contexts. Our protocol provides detailed step-by-step instructions, troubleshooting notes, and highlighted critical steps derived from extensive laboratory experience. It also includes comprehensive data analysis, including an in-house Python script to facilitate data processing.
Institutional permissions
The animal care and experiment in this protocol were carefully reviewed and approved by Kanazawa University’s ethics committee (Ethical Approval no. AP20-006). Researchers using this protocol must get the necessary permissions from their own institutions.
Tissue sample preparation
Timing: 4 h
1.
Preparation of C57BL6/J mice.
a.
Select 6 mice (3 for room temperature control and 3 for acute cold exposure) with similar age and body weight.
b.
Put each mouse in a single housing with food and water access for one week for acclimatization.
2.
Exposure to acute cold (4°C for 3 hours).
a.
Sequentially put the three mice for acute cold exposure into the cold chamber (4°C) with only water access (at least 10 minutes apart from each other).
b.
After 3 hours, immediately sacrifice the mice by decerebration.
c.
Take out the brown adipose tissue within 1 min.
d.
Cut the tissue into 4 pieces and put them in the serum tube.
e.
Freeze the samples with liquid nitrogen.
CRITICAL:
Immediate preparation and fixation of BAT tissue is essential to conserve the cysteine modifications. The separation of the starting time of cold exposure may provide the time for immediate sacrifice and preparation of BAT tissue.

Step-by-step method details
Labeling of reduced and oxidized cysteine residues by differential alkylation
Timing: 1 day
1.
Protein extraction from the tissue samples.
a.
Add 500 μL of pre-chilled
Tissue lysis buffer
to the 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube.
b.
Put the frozen tissue pieces into the tube.
c.
Homogenize with a handheld tissue grinder on ice until there are no visible tissue pieces.
d.
Transfer the homogenates to the new 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes.
e.
Sonicate 10 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C.
f.
Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 30 minutes at 4°C, collect the supernatant.
g.
Measure the protein concentration of each sample using DC Protein Assay Kit II from BIO-RAD.
i.
Prepare Reagent A′ by mixing Reagent A and Reagent S in 50:1 ratio.
ii.
Prepare and dilute Albumin protein standard (2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625 μg/ μL).
iii.
Prepare sample dilutions (2 to 3 times dilution).
iv.
Dispense 25 μL of Reagent A′, 5 μL of standards/samples, and 200 μL of Reagent B sequentially into each well of transparent 96-well plate.
v.
Incubate 15 minutes at room temperature and measure the absorbance at 650–750 nm.
2.
Labeling cysteine thiols (reduced cysteine residues) using N-ethylmaleimide (NEM).
a.
Prepare the 50 mL conical centrifuge tube for each sample and cover it with aluminum foil.
b.
Prepare and dilute the samples with
PBS buffer, pH 7.3,
to obtain a total protein of 2 mg per sample, and add NEM as the same mass as the protein content, with the final volume of 1 mL.
c.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
3.
Protein precipitation using methanol/chloroform.
a.
Add 4 mL of methanol to 1 mL volume of the previous sample mix and vortex for 10 seconds.
b.
Add 1 mL of chloroform to the sample and vortex for 10 seconds.
c.
Add 3 mL of ultrapure water (the sample should look cloudy) and vortex for 10 seconds.
d.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 2 minutes at room temperature.
e.
Discard the top aqueous layer. Protein exists between layers and is visible as a thin wafer.
f.
Add 4 mL of methanol and vortex for 10 seconds.
g.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 3 minutes at room temperature.
h.
Remove as much methanol as possible without disturbing the pellet.
i.
Open the lid of the tube and incubate at 37°C for 3 minutes to dry.
4.
Labeling of the oxidized cysteine residues using biotin-PEAC5-maleimide (BPM).
a.
Resuspend the pellet in 426.8 μL of 5 mM
TCEP solution, pH 7.7
.
b.
Incubate at 56°C for 30 minutes, followed by 15 minutes at room temperature.
c.
Add 73.2 μL of
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide stock solution
(Final biotin-PEAC5-maleimide concentration: 2.5 mM in 500 μL).
d.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
e.
Add 426.8 μL of 5 mM
TCEP solution, pH 7.7.
f.
Add 73.2 μL of
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide stock solution.
g.
Incubate at 37°C for 1 hour.
5.
Protein precipitation using methanol/chloroform.
a.
Add 4 mL of methanol to 1 mL of the previous sample mix and vortex for 10 seconds.
b.
Add 1 mL of chloroform to the sample and vortex for 10 seconds.
c.
Add 3 mL of ultrapure water (the sample should look cloudy) and vortex for 10 seconds
d.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 2 minutes at room temperature.
e.
Discard the top aqueous layer. Protein exists between layers and is visible as a thin wafer.
f.
Add 4 mL of methanol and vortex for 10 seconds.
g.
Centrifuge at 14,000 x g for 3 minutes at room temperature.
h.
Remove as much methanol as possible without disturbing the pellet
i.
Open the lid of the tube and incubate at 37°C for 3 minutes to dry.
CRITICAL:
All these steps require protection from light to prevent degradation of the biotin-peac5-maleimide, n-ethylmaleimide, and to avoid unwanted side reactions.
Note:
N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) completes its reaction kinetics within 15 minutes at neutral pH, and the reaction is irreversible.
5
,
6
Furthermore, its rapid reaction rate reduces the need to use large molar excesses.
6
This offers a significant advantage over one of the most common alkylating reagents, the haloalkane iodoacetamide (IAM), which requires a basic pH (above pH 8)
7
and incubation times of 4 to 6 h with a large molar excess of IAM (up to 1000 times that of protein cysteine).
8
Additionally, the reactions with IAM to form thioethers are often incomplete under these conditions and are not irreversible.
9
,
10
Note:
Biotin-PEAC5-maleimide (BPM) has a shorter and less bulky spacer arm, which reduces steric hindrance and makes it a more compact label in comparison to Maleimide-PEG2/11-maleimide. This compactness enhances accessibility to buried cysteine residues.
Pause point:
At this point, the peptide samples can be stored at 4°C for less than 24 h or at −80°C for less than one month.
In-solution trypsin digestion of labeled proteins
Timing: 3 days
6.
Denaturation of proteins by urea.
a.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 μL of
Trypsin digestion buffer with urea.
b.
Sonicate 5 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C.
c.
Incubate at 60°C for 1 hour.
d.
Allow the samples to cool down at room temperature (about 15 min).
e.
Add 3.5 mL of
Trypsin digestion buffer
(to decrease the urea concentration to 1 M).
f.
Sonicate 5 times (37 kHz, 10-sec pulse with 5-sec interval) at 4°C (Repeat this step until there are no insoluble substances that can be seen by the naked eye).
g.
Determine the protein concentration as in Step 1G.
h.
Transfer 1 mg of denatured proteins to new 50 mL conical centrifuge tubes.
7.
Digestion of denatured proteins by trypsin.
a.
Add 16.7 μg (41.75 μL) of sequencing-grade trypsin (1:60, 1 μg of Trypsin for 60 μg of protein) to each tube.
b.
Incubate at 37°C for 16 hours (can extend up to 18 hours).
c.
Add 16.7 μg (41.75 μL) of sequencing-grade trypsin to each tube again.
d.
Incubate at 37°C for 4 hours.
e.
Stop the trypsin digestion activity by adding
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
to the digestion mix until the solution reaches a pH below 4.
f.
Use a pH test strip to verify the pH of the solution. (2–3 times the volume of the sample mix may be needed).
8.
Concentration of digested peptides by vacuum centrifugation.
a.
Aliquot the sample mix to 1.5 mL centrifuge tubes (up to 1 mL in each 1.5 mL centrifuge tube).
b.
Centrifuge at 20,000 x g for 20 minutes at room temperature.
c.
Transfer the supernatant (about 500 μL) to a new 1.5 mL centrifuge tube.
d.
Resuspend the pellet in the previous 1.5 mL centrifuge tube by adding 100 μL of
0.1% Trifluoroacetic acid solution
and pipetting.
e.
Centrifuge at 20,000 x g for 20 minutes at room temperature.
f.
Transfer the supernatant (about 500 μL) to a new 1.5 mL centrifuge tube (Do not disturb the pellet).
g.
Concentrate each sample by vacuum centrifugation (SpeedVac) until only jelly-like fluid remains (may take up to 18–24 hours to dry).
CRITICAL:
It is crucial to open the microcentrifuge tube caps when speed-vacuuming to allow the solvent to evaporate.
CRITICAL:
The samples may suck out when the centrifugation is turned off prior to pressure stabilization. Let the pressure equalize before turning off the centrifugation to take out the samples.
Pause point:
At this point, the peptide samples can be stored at 4°C for less than 24 h or at −80°C for less than one month.

Expected outcomes
A successful experiment is expected to yield around 30,000 peptides per tissue sample, including approximately 1,500 peptides containing cysteine residues and about 600 cysteine-containing proteins from a 100 μg input loaded onto the LC-MS system. In brown adipose tissue samples, we typically detect roughly 500 oxidized cysteine residues and about 1,000 reduced cysteine residues. Please note that these numbers may vary by the characteristics of the samples.

Limitations
Our protocol, which consists of a double alkylation using both NEM and BPM, enables the identification of not only oxidized cysteine residues but also reduced and unlabeled cysteine residues. This direct detection of both oxidized and reduced cysteines allows us to detect not only oxidative stress but also reductive stress cysteine targets under specific stimuli. However, the number of cysteine residues that can be detected may significantly decrease without avidin enrichment. Previous studies,
2
,
3
,
4
together with the current method, face a common challenge in accurately quantifying reversibly oxidized cysteine residues with S-persulfidation (S-SH). The NEM can react with the thiol group in S-persulfidated cysteines (S-S-NEM), resulting in their misidentification as reduced cysteines (S-NEM) instead of oxidized cysteines. Future cysteine redoxome profiling should employ selective labeling techniques to ensure accurate identification.
Troubleshooting
Problem 1
Very few cysteine peptides are identified/quantified after completing the protocol.
Potential solution
•
Use the fresh tissue samples (immediately after sacrifice).
•
Increase protein lysate input to at least 3 mg per sample (increase volume or lysate concentration in step 2c).
•
Completely redissolve the pellet after methanol/chloroform precipitation.
Problem 2
In step 4a, 6a and 6f, the precipitated pellets are not redissolved completely.
Potential solution
•
Resuspend with vigorous pipetting.
•
Try to sonicate the solution using 37 kHz at 4°C for 5 – 10 minutes (repeat if required).
Problem 3
Very few oxidized and reduced cysteines are identified after completing the protocol.
Potential solution
•
Use the fresh NEM and BPM solution.
•
Recheck and adjust the pH of the solution to the optimal pH.
•
Increase the incubation time of NEM and BPM.
Problem 4
It takes a very long time to dry the peptide sample using SpeedVac.
Potential solution
•
Check air/vapor outlet of the machine is not clogged.
•
Check the pressure gauge to confirm the vacuum effect.
•
Try to separate the samples into many tubes with smaller liquid volumes.
Problem 5
The Aurora column clogged during the LC-MS run.
Potential solution
•
Try to increase the fractionation from 5 fractions to 8 fractions at Step 10k.
•
Try to decrease the peptide amount prepared for LC-MS analysis at Step 9b.
